questions.answer: A 2-hour battery at ERCOT's hub average (ercot:HB_HUBAVG) earned a total of 51.07 USD/kW on the day-ahead strategy over the 12 local months 2025-10 to 2026-09. This is the sum of the 12 monthly dayahead_2h_revenue_total values (battery_stack_monthly, derived), reported by calendar month in Central time. The monthly mean over the same 12 months is 4.26 USD/kW (battery_stack_monthly). The best month was 2026-01 at 11.33 USD/kW and the weakest was 2026-02 at 2.20 USD/kW. All 365 days in the period were held and none were left out (battery_stack_monthly). Method: energy plus ancillary services at day-ahead prices, per kW of rated power, with a price-taking battery and no capacity payment. These are modeled revenues, not measured ones.

questions.question: What did a 4-hour battery with perfect foresight at ERCOT's hub average earn in total in calendar year 2021, the year of Winter Storm Uri, in USD per kW?
questions.answer: A 4-hour battery with perfect foresight at ERCOT's hub average (ercot:HB_HUBAVG) earned about 3,431 USD/kW in total in calendar year 2021 (battery_stack_monthly, derived). That is the sum of the 12 monthly values of foresight_4h_revenue_total_usd_per_mw, 3430.56 USD/kW, covering energy plus ancillary services. All 365 days of the year were held (battery_stack_monthly). The months are local (Central time). February 2021, Winter Storm Uri, alone was 3115.95 USD/kW (battery_stack_monthly). The other ten months from March to December together were 298.05 USD/kW, and January was 16.55 USD/kW (battery_stack_monthly). Perfect foresight is an upper bound. The battery is modelled as a price taker, so the figure is overstated. It includes no capacity payment.

questions.answer: May 2025 earned the most. A 4-hour battery with perfect foresight at ERCOT's HB_HUBAVG earned 12,926.25 USD/MW (battery_stack_monthly, variable foresight_4h_revenue_total_usd_per_mw). That is energy plus ancillary services for the month, for 1 MW of rated power. The month is the local month, labelled 2025-05-01 UTC. All 31 of its 31 days were held (battery_stack_monthly). The next highest 2025 month was April, at 8,460.90 USD/MW (battery_stack_monthly). Perfect foresight is an upper bound, and the battery is modelled as a price taker. This is a derived table.

questions.question: In calendar year 2025, how much energy revenue did a 4-hour battery on the day-ahead strategy at CAISO's SP15 hub earn, in USD per kW?
questions.answer: A 4-hour battery on the day-ahead strategy at CAISO's SP15 hub (TH_SP15_GEN-APND) earned about 42.5 USD/kW of energy revenue in calendar year 2025 (battery_stack_monthly, derived). This is the sum of the twelve monthly values of dayahead_4h_revenue_energy_usd_per_mw for local months January to December 2025 (Pacific time). It is per kW of rated power. The table's USD/MW sum is 42,503.77. The table counts 362 days held of 365 (battery_stack_monthly). The 3 missing days, in April 2025, were left out because ancillary prices were missing: April has 27 days held of 30. A month's revenue covers its held days only. This is a modeled figure with round trip 0.86 and a price-taker battery. It excludes ancillary services and capacity payments.

I read peaker_revenue_per_mw as margin over fuel because the table's gross sales figure, peaker_sales_per_mw, is larger at 120,471 USD/MW for the same year. The table's notes do not state this outright.

# SPP: the written layer

## What this grid is and who runs it

The Southwest Power Pool (SPP) runs the power grid and wholesale market across the central Great Plains, from the Dakotas and Montana south through Nebraska, Kansas and Oklahoma to parts of Texas, New Mexico, Arkansas and Louisiana (SPP, https://www.spp.org/about-us/fast-facts/). It owns no power plants: it schedules the plants that its members own, keeps supply equal to demand, and plans transmission. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) approves its market rules.

Sources: https://www.spp.org/about-us/ ; https://www.spp.org/about-us/fast-facts/ ; https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/delivery-to-consumers.php

## How its market sets prices

SPP's market, the Integrated Marketplace, has a day-ahead market, where power for each hour of tomorrow is bought and sold today, and a real-time market, where plants are dispatched every few minutes. Prices are set at each location (locational marginal prices) and summarized at trading hubs; this page uses the SPP North Hub. SPP has no capacity auction: its members must show they have enough capacity themselves.

Sources: https://www.spp.org/about-us/ ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/wholesale/

## What makes it different

Wind. The Great Plains are among the windiest places in the country, and on windy nights wind can supply a large share of SPP's power (SPP, https://www.spp.org/about-us/fast-facts/), pushing some prices to zero or below. Because the wind is strongest far from cities, getting it to customers depends on long transmission lines, and SPP curtails wind when the lines are full: the curtailment tracker on this site shows it.

Sources: https://www.spp.org/about-us/fast-facts/ ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/dashboard/electric_overview/balancing_authority/SWPP

## A short history

- **1941:** Utilities in the region pool their power to keep an aluminum plant in Arkansas running for the war effort; SPP grows from this pool (SPP, https://www.spp.org/news-list/spp-celebrates-20-years-as-an-rto-with-growth-and-added-value-for-members/).
- **2014:** SPP launches the Integrated Marketplace, with day-ahead and real-time markets (SPP, https://www.spp.org/about-us/fast-facts/).
- **2021-02-15:** During Winter Storm Uri, SPP directs utilities to cut power to some customers to protect the grid (SPP, https://spp.org/documents/65037/comprehensive%20review%20of%20spp's%20response%20to%20the%20feb.%202021%20winter%20storm%202021%2007%2019.pdf).

Sources: https://www.spp.org/about-us/ ; https://www.spp.org/about-us/fast-facts/

## Glossary

- **Balancing authority:** the organization that keeps supply and demand equal in an area. EIA reports SPP as balancing authority SWPP.
- **Demand:** how much electricity customers are using, in megawatts (MW).
- **Megawatt (MW) and megawatt-hour (MWh):** a megawatt is a rate of power; a megawatt-hour is one megawatt for one hour, an amount of energy.
- **Net generation:** the power plants produce, minus what they use themselves.
- **Day-ahead market:** trades for each hour of tomorrow, agreed today.
- **Real-time market:** the price paid for power at the moment it is delivered.
- **Integrated Marketplace:** SPP's day-ahead and real-time markets.
- **Hub:** an average of many grid locations' prices, used as one reference price; this page uses the SPP North Hub.
- **Curtailment:** turning down wind or solar that could have produced, because the grid cannot use or move the power.
- **Carbon intensity:** the carbon dioxide released per megawatt-hour of electricity, in kilograms of CO2 per MWh.

Sources: https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/about ; https://www.spp.org/about-us/fast-facts/

# MISO: the written layer

## What this grid is and who runs it

The Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) runs the power grid and wholesale market across much of the middle of the country, from Minnesota, Wisconsin and Michigan south through Iowa, Illinois, Indiana and Missouri to Arkansas, Mississippi, Louisiana and East Texas, and into the Canadian province of Manitoba (MISO, https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/). It owns no power plants: it schedules the plants that its members own, keeps supply equal to demand, and plans transmission. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) approves its market rules.

Sources: https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/ ; https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/delivery-to-consumers.php

## How its market sets prices

MISO runs a day-ahead market, where power for each hour of tomorrow is bought and sold today, and a real-time market, where plants are dispatched every few minutes. Prices are set at each location (locational marginal prices) and summarized at trading hubs; this page uses the Indiana Hub. MISO also holds a yearly capacity auction for the coming planning year.

Sources: https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/ ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/wholesale/

## What makes it different

The north-south seam. MISO grew in two parts: the original northern footprint, and MISO South (Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and East Texas), which joined in 2013. The two are tied together by a narrow set of transmission links, so power often cannot flow freely between north and south, and prices on each side can differ. The north has a lot of wind and coal; the south has more natural gas and nuclear.

Sources: https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/ ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/dashboard/electric_overview/balancing_authority/MISO

## A short history

- **2001-12-20:** The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission approves MISO as the first regional transmission organization (RTO) in the United States (MISO, https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/industry-foundations/miso-history/).
- **2005-04-01:** MISO opens its day-ahead and real-time energy markets (FERC, https://ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2020-05/miso-06-30-05.pdf).
- **2013-12-19:** Utilities in Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and East Texas join MISO as MISO South (FERC, https://ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2020-05/E-4_84.pdf).

Sources: https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/

## Glossary

- **Balancing authority:** the organization that keeps supply and demand equal in an area. EIA reports MISO as balancing authority MISO.
- **Regional transmission organization (RTO):** a grid operator that runs transmission and markets across several states.
- **Demand:** how much electricity customers are using, in megawatts (MW).
- **Megawatt (MW) and megawatt-hour (MWh):** a megawatt is a rate of power; a megawatt-hour is one megawatt for one hour, an amount of energy.
- **Net generation:** the power plants produce, minus what they use themselves.
- **Day-ahead market:** trades for each hour of tomorrow, agreed today.
- **Real-time market:** the price paid for power at the moment it is delivered.
- **Hub:** an average of many grid locations' prices, used as one reference price; this page uses the Indiana Hub.
- **Seam:** a boundary between parts of the grid where power cannot flow freely.
- **Carbon intensity:** the carbon dioxide released per megawatt-hour of electricity, in kilograms of CO2 per MWh.

Sources: https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/about ; https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/

questions.question: In June 2026, how much higher or lower was the load-weighted real-time price at ERCOT's hub average than at CAISO's SP15 hub, in USD per MWh?
questions.answer: In June 2026, ERCOT's hub average (HB_HUBAVG) had a load-weighted real-time price 15.71 USD/MWh higher than CAISO's SP15 hub (cost_of_power_monthly, derived table). The ERCOT figure was 29.40 USD/MWh and the CAISO TH_SP15_GEN-APND figure was 13.69 USD/MWh. The 15.71 difference is the compare tool's ERCOT-minus-CAISO result. Both are for the local month of June, and the table holds 720 real-time hours of 720 in the month for each hub, so the month is complete. Load weighting uses hourly price times EIA-930 demand. This is wholesale energy only.
